stories.title: India moves a step closer to owning fighter-jet engine technology, as the Safran-GTRE deal for its stealth jet nears final government approval
key_points: The Safran-GTRE joint venture to build the engine for India's **AMCA Mark-2** stealth fighter is nearing approval from India's top security body, the **CCS**.
Clearance is expected **before August 15**, India's Independence Day.
The engine targets **110–130 kilonewtons (kN)** of thrust — starting at 120 kN, later uprated to **140 kN**.
**Nine prototype engines** are planned to be built and certified under the deal.
This would be the **first time India owns full intellectual property** in an advanced fighter jet engine — something it has never had before.
stories.background: The **AMCA (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft)** is India's own fifth-generation stealth fighter program, run by defence research body **DRDO**. A long-standing weakness of India's fighter jet ambitions has been engines: India has always had to buy or license foreign engines (from Russia, the US, or France) and has never owned the underlying technology outright. **GTRE (Gas Turbine Research Establishment)**, DRDO's engine-design arm, has partnered with French aerospace giant **Safran** to co-develop a new high-thrust engine specifically for the stealthier AMCA Mark-2 variant. The proposal now needs sign-off from India's **Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS)**, the top government body that approves major defence deals, chaired by the Prime Minister.
stories.what_happened: A joint venture proposal between **Safran** and **DRDO's GTRE** is nearing final approval from India's **Cabinet Committee on Security**, with clearance expected **ahead of August 15**. Once approved, it will allow the two sides to open **final negotiations** and sign a formal cooperation contract. The deal covers a new turbofan engine in the **110–130 kN thrust class**, built specifically to power the **AMCA Mark-2**, the more advanced stealth version of India's homegrown fighter jet. The engine is planned to start at **120 kN** of thrust with a later **140 kN** uprated version, and the program calls for **nine prototype engines** to be built and certified. Officials and defence analysts describe the deal's biggest significance as intellectual property: for the first time, India would **own the full IP** for an advanced fighter engine, rather than licensing or importing the technology.
stories.why_it_matters: Fighter jet engines are one of the hardest technologies to master, and owning the IP outright — instead of depending on foreign suppliers — is a major step toward genuine defence self-reliance, reducing India's exposure to export restrictions or supply disruptions from other countries.
stories.ripple_effects: A successful deal strengthens India-France defence ties and could position Safran for further Indian contracts, while boosting India's push to eventually export the AMCA or its engine technology to other countries. It also raises the stakes for GTRE and India's broader aerospace manufacturing base, which would need to scale up to build and certify nine prototype engines.
stories.why_now: The approval is being pushed to land before August 15, India's Independence Day — a symbolically significant date for a deal framed around defence self-reliance.
stories.watch_next: Whether the CCS formally signs off before August 15, followed by the start of contract negotiations between Safran and GTRE.

key_terms.definition: A unit of thrust force used to measure jet engine power — higher kN means a more powerful engine.
India's top government body, chaired by the Prime Minister, that approves major defence and security deals.

stories.the_lesson: In defence technology, owning the underlying intellectual property matters more than just having access to the equipment — a country that can only buy or license a technology stays dependent on the seller, while owning the IP means being able to build, modify, and export it independently.
stories.market_link: Positive for Indian defence and aerospace manufacturers linked to the AMCA program, and for Safran's defence engine business.

stories.title: RBI turns notably more upbeat on India's economy as the worst-feared damage from the Iran war fails to materialize
key_points: RBI held its benchmark **repo rate at 5.25%** for a **fourth straight meeting**, with all six policy committee members voting to hold.
Vehicle sales are at **record levels**, credit growth has hit a **two-year high**, and **GST receipts are rising at a double-digit pace**.
Inflation ticked up slightly last month but stayed **inside RBI's 2%–6% comfort band**.
Five months ago, the Iran war had raised fears of an **inflation spike and downturn** in India — those fears have **'so far failed to materialize.'**
RBI still flags the **ongoing Iran war and a deficient monsoon** as risks to watch.
stories.background: The **repo rate** is the interest rate at which India's central bank, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, lends to commercial banks — it's the main lever RBI uses to control inflation and growth: raise it to cool the economy, cut it to stimulate. When the Iran-Israel-US war broke out roughly five months ago, it pushed global oil prices higher and unsettled markets, since India imports most of its oil and a spike in crude prices usually feeds directly into inflation and India's import bill. RBI, headed by Governor **Sanjay Malhotra**, has been watching that risk closely in its monthly economic reports ever since.
stories.what_happened: India's central bank sounded **notably more confident** about the economy in its latest monthly report, five months after the Iran war first raised fears of an inflation spike and a broader slowdown. The **Monetary Policy Committee**, a six-member panel that sets interest rates, voted **unanimously** to hold the repo rate at **5.25%** for a **fourth consecutive meeting**, predicting inflation will ease further while growth stays resilient. The report points to concrete strength in demand: **vehicle sales at record levels**, **credit growth at a two-year high**, and **GST (India's national goods-and-services tax) receipts rising at a double-digit pace**. Inflation did pick up slightly last month, but it remained comfortably inside RBI's official **2%–6% tolerance band**. RBI's report still flags two live risks — the **unresolved Iran war** (which could yet push energy prices higher) and a **deficient monsoon**, since weak rains hurt farm output and rural spending.
stories.why_it_matters: This is RBI publicly signaling that a real external shock — a war thousands of miles away that could have spiked India's oil import bill and inflation — has so far been absorbed without derailing the economy, which matters for confidence, borrowing costs, and how aggressively the central bank might act if things change.
stories.ripple_effects: A steady rate and an upbeat tone typically support stock market sentiment, keep borrowing costs stable for consumers and businesses, and reduce pressure on the rupee. It also means EMIs (loan repayments) on home, auto, and personal loans are likely to stay unchanged for now rather than rise or fall.
stories.why_now: The report was published today as RBI's regular monthly economic assessment, timed roughly five months after the Iran war began — enough time for policymakers to judge whether the feared damage actually showed up in the data.
stories.watch_next: RBI's next full policy meeting and rate decision, plus how India's monsoon rainfall totals land over the rest of the season — a weak monsoon could reverse today's optimistic tone.

key_terms.definition: The interest rate at which India's central bank lends to commercial banks — the main tool it uses to control inflation and growth.
Goods and Services Tax — India's nationwide indirect tax on the sale of goods and services; rising GST collections signal strong economic activity.

stories.the_lesson: Central banks watch external shocks not just for their headline severity but for whether they actually show up in hard data like inflation and demand — a scary-sounding risk that doesn't translate into real economic damage gets downgraded in policy language, which is itself useful information for markets.
stories.market_link: A steady rate and upbeat RBI tone is generally supportive for Indian equities and the rupee; watch bank and auto stocks, which are sensitive to credit growth and vehicle sales trends cited in the report.

stories.title: India's retail inflation hits a 19-month high of 4.45% in July, driven by pricier food
key_points: **Consumer price index (CPI) inflation** rose to **4.45% in July**, up from 4.38% in June — the **highest reading in 19 months**.
**Food inflation** was the main driver, climbing to **5.52%** from 5.32% the previous month.
This is the **second straight month** that inflation has stayed above the **RBI's 4% target**, after 16 months of running below it.
The RBI itself expects headline inflation to keep rising and **peak near 5.9% in the October-December quarter**.
Data was released by the **National Statistics Office (NSO)** on August 12.
stories.background: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures how much prices for a broad basket of everyday goods and services — like food, fuel and housing — have changed for typical households, and it's India's main gauge of retail inflation. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) targets keeping CPI inflation around 4%, using it as the main input for interest-rate decisions. Just a week earlier, the RBI's rate-setting committee had held its key policy rate steady at 5.25% for a fourth straight meeting, citing a wish for 'greater clarity' on where inflation was heading before acting either way.
stories.what_happened: The National Statistics Office reported that India's retail inflation rose to 4.45% in July, its highest level in 19 months and up from 4.38% in June. The increase was mainly driven by food prices, where inflation rose to 5.52% from 5.32% the month before. This marks the second consecutive month inflation has printed above the RBI's 4% target, following sixteen straight months where it had stayed below that level. The RBI's own projections, released alongside its August rate decision, anticipate inflation will keep climbing in the near term and peak around 5.9% in the October-December quarter of this fiscal year, before easing again.
stories.why_it_matters: Inflation eating into household budgets is one of the most direct ways an economic trend is felt by ordinary people, especially through food costs, which weigh heaviest on lower-income families. It also narrows the RBI's room to cut interest rates to support growth, since doing so while inflation is already running hot risks making prices rise even faster.
stories.ripple_effects: Higher food inflation typically hits rural and lower-income households hardest, since they spend a larger share of their income on food. For markets, a hotter inflation print reduces the odds of an RBI rate cut at its October meeting, which matters for borrowing costs on everything from home loans to corporate credit, and can affect how foreign investors view Indian bonds.
stories.why_now: The data covers July and was released by the NSO on August 12, arriving just a week after the RBI's own rate decision cited inflation uncertainty as the reason for holding rates steady.
stories.watch_next: Whether food prices continue climbing into the RBI's projected 5.9% peak in the October-December quarter, and how that shapes the central bank's rate decision at its next meeting, October 5-7.

key_terms.definition: A measure of how much prices for a typical basket of goods and services have risen over time — India's main gauge of retail inflation.

stories.the_lesson: Inflation data is backward-looking but forward-steering: a single month's higher-than-expected print can shift a central bank's entire near-term interest-rate plan, because it changes how much room policymakers feel they have to support growth without letting prices spiral.
stories.market_link: Hotter-than-expected inflation reduces the odds of an RBI rate cut, which matters for rate-sensitive sectors like banks, NBFCs, autos and real estate, and for how foreign investors price Indian government bonds.

stories.title: Jharkhand police file cases against 600 protesters after violent clashes at recruitment-exam demonstration
key_points: Jharkhand Police have booked **600 protesters** — **100 named, 500 unidentified** — over violence during an Assembly 'gherao' march in Ranchi on August 10.
The protest is over alleged **irregularities and paper leaks** in JPSC and JSSC recruitment exams, now in its **20th day** of agitation.
Police used **lathi charges, tear gas and water cannons** to disperse the march; student leader Devendra Nath Mahto was detained.
Investigators are examining video, CCTV and drone footage, and may use **facial-recognition and AI-based tools** to identify protesters.
The crackdown forced Jharkhand's Assembly Speaker to **adjourn the House twice** after BJP MLAs protested the police action.
stories.background: For nearly three weeks, students and job aspirants have been protesting alleged irregularities in exams run by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC) — the state bodies that conduct recruitment tests for government jobs. Their core demand is an independent probe, ideally by the CBI or a panel of retired High Court judges from outside Jharkhand, into alleged paper leaks and irregularities, along with cancellation of the affected exams. The protests escalated on August 10 into a march to gherao (surround) the state Legislative Assembly in Ranchi.
stories.what_happened: Jharkhand Police have registered FIRs against roughly 600 people over alleged violence during the August 10 march on the Assembly, naming 100 individuals directly and booking another 500 as unidentified. Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto, who was leading the demonstration, was among those detained by police, who used lathi charges, tear gas shells and water cannons to break up the crowd. Investigators say they are reviewing video footage, CCTV recordings and drone camera footage from the protest site, and have signaled that facial-recognition and AI-based identification technology may be used if needed to identify additional suspects. The police action has spilled into state politics: opposition BJP MLAs disrupted assembly proceedings over the crackdown, forcing the Speaker to adjourn the House twice.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a test of how a state government balances public order against the right to protest — mass FIRs naming 500 unidentified people, combined with talk of facial recognition, raise real questions about surveillance overreach against demonstrators exercising a legitimate grievance about exam fairness.
stories.ripple_effects: The case adds to youth unemployment and exam-fairness frustrations that have flared in several Indian states in recent years. If facial-recognition tools are actually deployed against protesters, it could set a precedent other states watch closely, and fuel a broader civil-liberties debate around policing of student movements.
stories.why_now: The FIRs were filed as police reviewed footage from the August 10 clash, with the announcement landing today as the underlying protest movement enters its 20th day with no resolution in sight.
stories.watch_next: Whether the state government agrees to the students' core demand — an independent CBI or judge-led probe into the JPSC/JSSC exam irregularities — or whether the protest movement continues to escalate.

key_terms.definition: A protest tactic, common in India, where demonstrators surround a building or officials to demand attention or block business as usual.

stories.the_lesson: When a government responds to a protest over institutional fairness with mass legal action against the protesters themselves, it often shifts the story from the original grievance to a new one about state power and surveillance — which can widen a local dispute into a bigger political fight.

stories.title: India's Monsoon Session of Parliament ends today, passing 11 bills after weeks of NEET-protest disruption

thread.previously: We reported the Opposition was blocking normal business, demanding Home Minister Amit Shah personally address the police response to the July 20 NEET-protest clash at Jantar Mantar, and that the standoff was eating into the Monsoon Session's last sitting days before its scheduled August 13 close.
thread.changed: The session has now ended on schedule — Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairman C P Radhakrishnan adjourned both Houses sine die today, with 11 bills passed, including the Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill by voice vote, despite disruptions continuing through the final days.

key_points: Parliament's **Monsoon Session** was adjourned **sine die** today, closing on its originally scheduled date.
**11 bills** were passed across both Houses over the course of the session.
The **Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill** cleared the Rajya Sabha by **voice vote** in the final sitting.
The session opened on **July 20** and was repeatedly disrupted by protests over the **NEET-UG paper leak** police crackdown.
The final Lok Sabha sitting opened with **Vande Mataram**, with PM Modi and Congress's Rahul Gandhi both present.
stories.background: "Sine die" adjournment means a legislative session ends completely with no date set to resume — different from a normal recess. This Monsoon Session began on **July 20** already under pressure, as the Opposition demanded Home Minister Amit Shah personally explain the police response to a **NEET-UG paper-leak protest** at Jantar Mantar that Delhi Police say injured roughly **60 protesters and 118 police personnel**. That standoff, alongside disputes like the contested **FCRA** bill (which lets government seize NGOs' foreign-funded assets and was instead referred to a joint parliamentary panel), repeatedly disrupted proceedings through the session.
stories.what_happened: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairman C P Radhakrishnan adjourned their respective Houses **sine die** on Thursday, officially closing the Monsoon Session. Despite the disruptions, both Houses together passed **11 bills** during the session, with the **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill** clearing the Rajya Sabha by voice vote in the closing sitting. The Lok Sabha's final day opened with six stanzas of **Vande Mataram**, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi both present in the chamber. The Opposition's core demand — that Amit Shah personally address the Jantar Mantar police-crackdown allegations — was never formally resolved on the floor before the session closed.
stories.why_it_matters: Whether contentious legislation like the FCRA bill, delimitation, or other pending items can move forward depends on Parliament actually functioning rather than getting stuck in walkouts — this closing tally is effectively the session's report card on productivity versus gridlock.
stories.ripple_effects: Bills not passed this session, including the still-pending FCRA legislation now with a joint panel, carry over to whenever Parliament next sits. The unresolved demand for Shah's statement on the NEET crackdown remains a live grievance the Opposition can keep raising.
stories.why_now: August 13 was the scheduled close date set when the session began on July 20, so today's sine die adjournment is the planned end, not an early cutoff.
stories.watch_next: Whether Amit Shah ultimately makes the statement Opposition MPs demanded, and what happens to the pending FCRA bill in the joint parliamentary panel.

key_terms.definition: Latin for "without a day" — when a legislative session is adjourned sine die, it ends completely with no date set to reconvene, unlike a normal recess.

stories.the_lesson: A legislative session can look chaotic in daily coverage — walkouts, adjournments, shouting matches — and still close having passed real legislation; disruption and output aren't mutually exclusive in how Parliament actually functions.

stories.title: Tata Trusts formally kicks off the search for Chandrasekaran's successor, with Tata Steel's T V Narendran an early frontrunner

thread.previously: We reported that after Chandrasekaran said he wouldn't seek reappointment, Tata Sons had to run its succession process for the first time since 2017 — and that the natural internal candidate, Noel Tata, already chairs Tata Trusts, which the group's 2022 rules block from also holding the Tata Sons chairmanship.
thread.changed: Tata Trusts has now formally passed a resolution to set up a five-member Selection Committee to recommend Chandrasekaran's successor, and Tata Steel CEO T V Narendran has emerged as an early frontrunner alongside Tata Sons CFO Saurabh Agrawal and Tata Motors chief Shailesh Chandra.

key_points: Tata Trusts passed a resolution to set up a **five-member Selection Committee** to recommend the next Tata Sons chairman.
**T V Narendran**, Tata Steel's global CEO and a 38-year Tata veteran, has emerged as an early frontrunner.
Other reported contenders include Tata Sons CFO **Saurabh Agrawal** and Tata Motors chief **Shailesh Chandra**.
**Noel Tata** could only step in as *interim* chairman in an emergency — he can't hold the job permanently while also chairing Tata Trusts.
The process formally begins just **days before** the group's **August 18** AGM, with no chairman yet named.
stories.background: Tata Sons, the holding company for the roughly **$165 billion** Tata Group, is majority-owned by two philanthropic bodies — the **Sir Dorabji Tata Trust** and **Sir Ratan Tata Trust** — which together control who becomes chairman. N. Chandrasekaran has led Tata Sons since **2017** and told the trusts on **August 12** that he will not seek reappointment when his term ends in **February 2027**. Under 2022 governance rules, the Tata Trusts chairman (currently Noel Tata) cannot simultaneously hold the Tata Sons chairmanship, which rules out the family's most obvious internal candidate from taking the job outright.
stories.what_happened: The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust's trustees passed a resolution to set up a **Selection Committee** "as soon as possible" to recommend a new Tata Sons chairman, as required under the company's Articles of Association. The committee will have **five members**: three jointly nominated by the two Tata Trusts, one from the Tata Sons board, and one independent outside member chosen by the board — with the two trusts also picking the committee's chair from among their three nominees. Early reporting names **T V Narendran**, Tata Steel's Global CEO and MD since 1988 with the group, as a leading contender, alongside Tata Sons CFO **Saurabh Agrawal** and Tata Motors MD/CEO **Shailesh Chandra**. Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts, can only step in as an *interim* Tata Sons chairman in exigent circumstances — not take the role permanently — under the same 2022 rules that created this succession puzzle in the first place.
stories.why_it_matters: Tata Sons' chairman effectively sets direction for one of India's largest conglomerates — spanning steel, autos, IT services and airlines, and employing hundreds of thousands of people — so how smoothly (or not) this process runs matters well beyond one boardroom.
stories.ripple_effects: Tata group stocks, some of which have already wobbled on succession uncertainty, are likely to keep reacting to news about frontrunners as the Selection Committee does its work. The trusts have a strong incentive to avoid a repeat of the bitter, public 2016 ouster of former chairman Cyrus Mistry, which badly damaged investor confidence at the time.
stories.why_now: The trusts had to move quickly because the group's AGM is scheduled for **August 18** — just days away — with no chairman currently in place.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Selection Committee names a recommended successor before or around the August 18 AGM.

key_terms.definition: Philanthropic trusts that together own roughly two-thirds of Tata Sons and, through that stake, control who leads the Tata Group.

stories.the_lesson: In founder-controlled conglomerates, succession isn't just about picking a capable executive — it runs through whatever governance rules the controlling shareholder wrote for itself, and those rules can rule out the "obvious" choice entirely.
stories.market_link: Tata group stocks (Tata Motors, Tata Steel, TCS, Tata Consumer) could see continued volatility as markets handicap succession candidates ahead of the August 18 AGM.

stories.title: ISRO launches AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird Block-2 — the heaviest satellite ever lifted from Indian soil
key_points: ISRO launched the **BlueBird Block-2** satellite on its heaviest rocket, the **LVM3-M6**, from Sriharikota at **8:55 AM IST**.
ISRO's chairman called it the **heaviest satellite ever lifted from Indian soil** using an Indian-built launcher.
The satellite separated and reached orbit after a roughly **15-minute flight**.
It's part of **AST SpaceMobile's** global constellation for **direct-to-mobile** connectivity — letting ordinary smartphones connect to satellites without special hardware.
stories.background: LVM3 (formerly known as GSLV Mk III) is ISRO's most powerful operational rocket, built to carry India's heaviest payloads and increasingly used to launch other countries' commercial satellites for a fee. AST SpaceMobile is a US company building a constellation of large low-Earth-orbit satellites designed to connect directly to regular, unmodified smartphones — filling in cellular 'dead zones' without needing special satellite phones. India's space program has been steadily building a commercial launch business alongside its own missions, competing for a slice of the growing global demand for satellite launches.
stories.what_happened: ISRO successfully launched the BlueBird Block-2 communication satellite on its LVM3-M6 rocket from Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, at 8:55 AM IST. After a flight of about 15 minutes, the satellite separated from the rocket and was placed into its intended orbit. ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan called it the heaviest satellite ever lifted off Indian soil by an Indian launch vehicle. The mission is part of AST SpaceMobile's global low-Earth-orbit constellation, which aims to provide direct-to-mobile satellite connectivity to ordinary phones.
stories.why_it_matters: This cements India's position as a serious commercial heavy-lift launch provider at a moment when demand for direct-to-phone satellite connectivity is surging worldwide, giving ISRO's commercial arm a shot at a growing revenue stream beyond government missions.
stories.ripple_effects: A successful heavy commercial launch can attract more foreign satellite operators to book future ISRO launches, and it advances a technology — direct-to-mobile satellite coverage — that could eventually bring basic phone signal to remote areas with no cell towers.
stories.why_now: It comes amid a global race among satellite operators, including AST SpaceMobile and rivals like Starlink's direct-to-cell service, to close mobile coverage gaps by connecting ordinary phones straight to satellites.
stories.watch_next: ISRO's next LVM3 commercial launches, and whether AST SpaceMobile's constellation moves toward commercial phone service.

key_terms.definition: Technology that lets an ordinary smartphone connect straight to a satellite for calls, texts, or data — no special satellite phone or extra hardware needed.
ISRO's most powerful operational rocket, used for its heaviest satellite payloads, including large commercial satellites for other countries.

stories.the_lesson: Space capability has become a commercial export industry, not just a national-prestige program — countries now earn real revenue by launching other nations' and companies' satellites.
stories.market_link: A positive signal for India's space sector and ISRO's commercial launch arm (NSIL) as global demand for satellite launches keeps growing.

stories.title: Bangladesh claws back to 175 for 2 on day two in Darwin, trailing Australia by just 23 runs
key_points: Bangladesh reached **175/2** after 50 overs on day two, having bowled Australia out for **198** in their first innings
**Mominul Haque (35 not out)** and **Tanzid Hasan (32 not out)** are steering a fightback that has trimmed the deficit to just **23 runs**
The platform follows **Hasan Mahmud's career-best 6 for 55**, which skittled Australia's first innings on day one
This is Bangladesh's **first-ever Test tour of Australia**, ending a 23-year wait for a red-ball series Down Under
Australia's **Mitchell Starc** became Test cricket's most successful left-arm bowler during the innings, passing Rangana Herath
stories.background: Bangladesh's tour of Australia is historic in itself — this is the first time the team has played a Test series in Australia, 23 years after first joining the small group of nations with Test status. The match is being played in Darwin, a venue known for hot, humid conditions that can behave differently to Australia's more familiar southern grounds. Bangladesh went into day one as heavy underdogs against an Australian side that includes veteran fast bowler Mitchell Starc, one of the most successful bowlers in the format's history.
stories.what_happened: On day one, Bangladesh's bowlers bundled Australia out for just 198, with fast bowler Hasan Mahmud claiming a career-best 6 for 55, and the tourists closed the day at 96 for 1 in reply. On day two, Bangladesh continued building on that platform, reaching 175 for 2 after 50 overs with Mominul Haque unbeaten on 35 and Tanzid Hasan unbeaten on 32, cutting the deficit to Australia's total to just 23 runs. During Australia's innings, veteran fast bowler Mitchell Starc passed Sri Lanka's Rangana Herath to become the most successful left-arm bowler in Test cricket history.
stories.why_it_matters: A first-innings lead, or even a small deficit, would be a landmark result for Bangladesh on their first-ever Test visit to Australia — a result that would rank among the biggest upsets of their Test history if it holds.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong showing here would boost Bangladesh's case for more regular Test tours to major cricket nations and lift their position in the World Test Championship standings. It would also raise fresh questions about Australia's depth outside their home comfort zone in more traditional conditions.
stories.why_now: The match is live and in progress, with day two's play having just concluded — the story is developing in real time as the tourists close in on Australia's total.
stories.watch_next: Whether Bangladesh can push past Australia's total of 198 and build a first-innings lead when play resumes on day three.
stories.the_lesson: In Test cricket, momentum built with the ball on day one can carry straight into a batting fightback on day two — a good bowling performance often sets up the platform for an unlikely result.

stories.title: Jasprit Bumrah ruled out of the Sri Lanka Tests as India hands uncapped Auqib Nabi a shock call-up
key_points: **Jasprit Bumrah** misses the two-match series as he continues recovering from a left-knee injury picked up in the England ODIs
**Shubman Gill** has been declared fit to captain the side after a finger scare in the warm-up match
**Auqib Nabi**, 26, earns his maiden India call-up after taking **104 wickets** across his last two Ranji Trophy seasons
KL Rahul is vice-captain; **Sai Sudharsan** is also out of the series with a fractured toe
The first Test starts **August 15** in Galle — India's first red-ball tour of Sri Lanka in **nine years**
stories.background: India last toured Sri Lanka for a Test series in 2017, when Virat Kohli's side completed a 3-0 clean sweep. This series is part of the 2025-27 World Test Championship (WTC) cycle, in which India currently sit fifth in the standings and Sri Lanka sixth. Bumrah, India's premier fast bowler, has been carefully managed through injuries in recent months, while allrounder Ravindra Jadeja's fitness has also been closely watched heading into this tour.
stories.what_happened: The BCCI announced a 15-member squad for the two-match Test series against Sri Lanka, naming Shubman Gill as captain and KL Rahul as vice-captain. Bumrah was left out entirely as he continues recovering from the knee injury sustained during India's ODI series in England, and uncapped fast bowler Auqib Nabi — who took 104 wickets in his last two Ranji Trophy seasons for Jammu and Kashmir, including 60 in this year's title-winning campaign — was named as his replacement. stories.why_it_matters: Losing your best fast bowler and a key top-order batter before a tough overseas series forces India to rebuild both its attack and batting order on the fly, while handing a completely uncapped bowler an immediate baptism in unfamiliar, spin-friendly conditions.
stories.ripple_effects: Auqib Nabi's selection could reshape India's fast-bowling depth chart heading into the WTC run-in, and how Gill manages both the captaincy and a patched-up bowling attack will be closely watched. A poor start could also increase pressure on India's position in the WTC standings.
stories.why_now: The squad announcement comes just two days before the series opener, giving the team its final answers on fitness and selection right before departure.
stories.watch_next: How Auqib Nabi performs in his Test debut at Galle, and whether Bumrah is fit to return for the second Test in Colombo.

key_terms.definition: India's premier domestic first-class cricket tournament, the main pathway for players to break into the national Test side.

stories.the_lesson: Depth in domestic cricket is what lets a team absorb the loss of a star player without collapsing — Auqib Nabi's 104 domestic wickets are exactly why he was ready when the call came.

thread.previously: As of yesterday, Sai Sudharsan had been ruled out with a toe fracture and Shubman Gill's own participation was in doubt after a finger injury in the warm-up match.

stories.title: Scotland thump Canada by 170 runs in Dundee rematch to boost their 2027 World Cup qualification hopes
key_points: Scotland beat Canada by **170 runs** in Dundee, posting **347/7** before bowling Canada out for just **177**.
Left-armer **Lyle Robertson** starred with **6 wickets for 52 runs**, earning Player of the Match.
The result comes just days after Scotland edged the same opponent by a much tighter **9 runs** in an earlier meeting.
The match was part of the **ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2**, a qualification pathway toward the 2027 World Cup.
stories.background: Scotland and Canada are both competing in the ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2, a multi-year qualifying league among associate cricket nations vying for a place at the 2027 Cricket World Cup. The two sides had already met earlier this month in a tight 9-run Scotland win, making this rematch a chance for Scotland to build a bigger points cushion.
stories.what_happened: Scotland posted a commanding **347 for 7** batting first at Forthill in Dundee, then bowled out Canada for just **177**, winning by **170 runs**. Left-arm bowler Lyle Robertson was the standout performer, taking **6 wickets for 52 runs** to earn Player of the Match honours. stories.title: BCCI seeks the Indian government's go-ahead before confirming a Bangladesh tour, as cricket ties stay strained
key_points: BCCI says it will approach the **Indian government** for formal clearance before confirming a tour of Bangladesh
Tensions began in **January 2026** when BCCI asked KKR to release Bangladeshi bowler Mustafizur Rahman from the IPL
Bangladesh's board (BCB) then **refused to travel to India** for the 2026 T20 World Cup, citing security advice
A recent visit by **BCB president Tamim Iqbal** to the BCCI's Bengaluru academy has revived hopes for the tour
The series was originally set for **August 2025** before being deferred to **September 2026**
stories.background: Cricket ties between India and Bangladesh soured amid the political turmoil in Bangladesh under its interim government led by Muhammad Yunus, feeding into a broader chill in bilateral relations. The flashpoint came when BCCI, citing violence against religious minorities in Bangladesh, asked Kolkata Knight Riders to release Bangladeshi pace bowler Mustafizur Rahman from their IPL 2026 squad — a request Bangladesh's board answered days later by pulling its national team out of traveling to India for the 2026 T20 World Cup over security concerns. Since then, ties have shown signs of thawing under new Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
stories.what_happened: BCCI sources say the board has locked in a proposed window for a six-match tour of Bangladesh but will not confirm it until it receives formal approval from the Indian government — standard practice for tours to countries where diplomatic sensitivities are in play. This follows a visit by BCB president Tamim Iqbal to the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, which cricket officials on both sides described as a positive step toward normalizing relations. The tour, originally scheduled for August 2025, was deferred by mutual agreement to September 2026 after the earlier diplomatic rupture.
stories.why_it_matters: Cricket between India and Bangladesh is not just sport — it has become a visible barometer of the two countries' broader political relationship, and a canceled or confirmed tour sends a real diplomatic signal beyond the pitch. Government sign-off requirements show how closely India treats sports diplomacy as an extension of foreign policy when relations are fragile.
stories.ripple_effects: A confirmed tour would be read as a genuine thaw in India-Bangladesh relations and give both boards' broadcast and sponsorship revenues a lift; a further delay or cancellation would be read as ties remaining fragile. Player availability and IPL contracts for Bangladeshi cricketers could also remain a flashpoint depending on how relations evolve.
stories.why_now: The tour window needs to be locked in soon given the September 2026 target date, forcing BCCI to seek government clearance now.
stories.watch_next: Watch for the Indian government's formal response and whether BCCI and BCB announce confirmed fixtures for the September window.
stories.the_lesson: When diplomatic relations between two countries sour, even seemingly unrelated institutions — like national cricket boards — end up needing government sign-off, because sport rarely stays separate from politics for long.

stories.title: India names Shubman Gill to captain the Sri Lanka Tests, with Bumrah and Jadeja's returns still hanging on fitness
key_points: BCCI named its **15-man Test squad** for the two-match Sri Lanka series, starting **August 15** in Galle

**Ravindra Jadeja** returns after being rested for the Afghanistan series in June
**Jasprit Bumrah**'s spot is contested — reports conflict on whether he's fully cleared or still assessing his knee
**Auqib Nabi**, a 26-year-old pacer from Jammu and Kashmir, gets a maiden call-up after **104 wickets** in two Ranji seasons
stories.background: India's Test side has been managing a wave of injuries through the middle of 2026, with fast bowler Jasprit Bumrah's fitness in particular being carefully managed by the BCCI's medical team since a knee issue first flared up around the T20 World Cup. The two-Test series against Sri Lanka — the first Test in Galle from August 15-19, the second in Colombo from August 23-27 — comes as India also manages the workload of veterans like Ravindra Jadeja, who sat out the Afghanistan series in June.

Ravindra Jadeja returns to the squad after his rest period, and uncapped domestic performer **Auqib Nabi** earns his first India call-up on the back of 104 wickets across his last two Ranji Trophy seasons. stories.why_it_matters: Bumrah is India's premier fast bowler and a genuine match-winner in Test cricket — his availability alone can swing a series, so his uncertain status is the single biggest storyline heading into the tour. The squad announcement also confirms India's leadership continuity under Gill after a period of speculation about his own fitness.

stories.title: Mitchell Starc becomes Test cricket's most successful left-arm bowler ever, passing Rangana Herath
key_points: Starc reached **434 Test wickets**, passing Sri Lanka's **Rangana Herath (433)** to become the most successful left-arm bowler in Test history.
He got there by dismissing Bangladesh opener **Shadman Islam** during the historic **Darwin Test**.
The milestone came in his **106th Test**, and fell on **International Left-Handers Day** (August 13).
Starc is now **level with Kapil Dev** on the all-time wicket-takers list, and just **six behind Dale Steyn's 439** for the top ten overall.
stories.background: Mitchell Starc has been Australia's frontline left-arm fast bowler for over a decade, known for swinging the new ball and reverse-swinging the old one. Left-arm bowlers face a quirk regardless of pace or style: there have simply been far fewer of them across cricket history than right-arm bowlers, which makes elite career wicket tallies rarer among them. Sri Lankan left-arm spinner **Rangana Herath** had held the left-arm wicket-taking record with 433 dismissals since his retirement. Starc reached the milestone during Australia's landmark first-ever home Test against Bangladesh, a fixture Bangladesh waited 23 years to secure.
stories.what_happened: During day two of the Australia-Bangladesh Test in Darwin, Mitchell Starc dismissed opener Shadman Islam to take his **434th Test wicket**, moving past Rangana Herath's **433** to become the leading left-arm bowler in Test cricket history. The milestone arrived in Starc's **106th Test appearance** and, fittingly, on **International Left-Handers Day**. The achievement also puts him level with India great **Kapil Dev** on the all-time wicket-takers list, and within six wickets of South Africa's **Dale Steyn (439)** for a place in the game's top ten leading wicket-takers overall, regardless of arm or bowling style.
stories.why_it_matters: This cements Starc's place among the greatest fast bowlers of his generation, and highlights how rare genuinely elite left-arm bowling careers are — there have been far fewer standout left-armers across Test history than right-armers, making a tally like this especially significant.
stories.ripple_effects: The milestone adds to the storyline of Australia's dominant bowling attack during a historic tour, and will likely fuel more discussion about where Starc ultimately ranks among all-time greats as he continues closing in on the top-ten wicket-takers list.
stories.why_now: It happened live during play on day two of the ongoing Darwin Test, cricket's first-ever meeting between Australia and Bangladesh on Australian soil.
stories.watch_next: Whether Starc can close the six-wicket gap to Dale Steyn's 439 before this series ends, and how far Australia push their advantage in the rest of the Darwin Test.

key_terms.definition: A bowler who delivers the ball with their left hand — rarer than right-arm bowlers across cricket history, which makes high career wicket tallies among left-armers especially notable.

stories.the_lesson: Longevity and consistency compound — Starc's record didn't come from one standout spell, but from turning up and taking wickets across 106 Tests over more than a decade.

stories.what_happened: Ashwin used his platform to name his personal 15-man India squad for the **2027 ODI World Cup**, more than a year out from the tournament. I would communicate and ask him to play all the first-class tournaments to make sure he is ready and primed to go to South Africa.'** He named **Kuldeep Yadav** as his first-choice spinner, with **Harshit Rana, Mohammed Siraj and Jasprit Bumrah** rounding out his pace attack, and listed **Shubman Gill, Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli** as certainties. stories.why_it_matters: Squad predictions this far out don't decide anything, but they crystallize a real selection debate India's selectors will eventually have to settle: whether to prioritize experienced names like Pant and Samson or lean into form and fitness, and whether an older-but-effective bowler like Bhuvneshwar Kumar still has a role in 2027.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect debate and pushback from fans and other pundits, especially over the Pant and Samson omissions, both established international wicketkeeper-batters. It also puts informal pressure on players like Bhuvneshwar Kumar to be visibly active in domestic cricket to keep the selection conversation alive.
stories.why_now: It comes as India's selection conversations are already active around the ongoing Test squad news, and pundit World Cup previews typically pick up steam whenever a marquee tournament is roughly a year or so away.
stories.watch_next: How India's actual selectors' picks evolve over the next year of ODI cricket, and whether Bhuvneshwar Kumar's domestic form in the coming season keeps him in the selection conversation.

key_terms.definition: One Day International — a format of cricket where each team bats for a maximum of 50 overs, the format used for the Cricket World Cup.

stories.the_lesson: Expert predictions made well ahead of a real decision are as much about framing the debate as forecasting the outcome — they surface the tradeoffs decision-makers will eventually have to weigh, even when the prediction itself won't come true exactly as stated.

stories.watch_next: The Eliminator between Manchester Super Giants and Sunrisers Leeds at The Oval on August 14, which decides who plays Trent Rockets in the August 16 final at Lord's.

stories.title: Bangladesh reach 96/1 at stumps, trailing Australia by just 102, after bowling the hosts out for 198
key_points: Bangladesh closed day one at **96/1**, trailing Australia's first-innings **198** by just **102 runs**.
**Mominul Haque and Tanzid Hasan** both finished the day not out, building a solid platform in reply.
Only **Mitchell Starc** looked genuinely threatening with the ball; the rest of Australia's attack, including Nathan Lyon, made little impact.
Bangladesh had earlier bowled Australia out for **198**, with **Hasan Mahmud** taking a career-best **6 for 55**.
It's Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years** — and they've taken the early honours.
stories.background: Bangladesh arrived in Australia for their first Test tour of the country in 23 years, historically one of the toughest assignments in world cricket given Australia's pace-friendly home conditions. At Marrara Stadium in Darwin, Australia won the toss and chose to bat first — the conventional move at a ground where the pitch typically gets harder to bat on as a match wears on. Instead, Bangladesh's pace attack dismantled the Australian batting order on day one.
stories.what_happened: Australia were bowled out for just 198 on the opening day, with Hasan Mahmud claiming a career-best 6 for 55 — his third Test five-wicket haul — as Bangladesh's fast bowlers took all 10 Australian wickets, only the second time that has happened in the team's Test history. Steve Smith top-scored for the hosts with 71 off 109 balls. In reply, Bangladesh reached 96 for 1 by stumps, trailing by just 102 runs, with Mominul Haque and Tanzid Hasan both unbeaten and looking well set. Starc was the one Australian bowler who consistently troubled the Bangladesh batters, but the rest of the attack — including veteran spinner Nathan Lyon — couldn't find similar impact as conditions eased through the day.
stories.why_it_matters: A team on just its second-ever Test tour of Australia dominating day one of the series opener is a genuinely rare result — it flips the psychological pressure onto the home side and gives Bangladesh a real chance to post a first-innings lead in only their sixth Test match in the country.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong start here could reshape expectations for the rest of this historic two-Test series, with the second Test following at Mackay from August 22-26. It's also a significant confidence boost for Bangladesh's fast-bowling pipeline, led by the uncapped-to-star rise of Hasan Mahmud.
stories.why_now: This is the direct continuation of day one's play, with Bangladesh's reply innings unfolding through the same session in which they finished bowling Australia out.
stories.watch_next: Whether Mominul Haque and Tanzid Hasan can extend their partnership on day two and push Bangladesh into a first-innings lead against Australia at home.
stories.the_lesson: In cricket as in many contests, winning the toss and choosing the 'conventional' option isn't a guarantee — conditions and execution on the day can matter far more than the textbook strategy.

stories.title: Root scraps England's midnight curfew in his first move as reinstated Test captain
key_points: Joe Root has **abolished England's midnight curfew** ahead of the Pakistan Test series.
It's his **first concrete decision** since being reinstated as Test captain.
Root says players should be trusted to **manage themselves like adults** off the field, just as they are on it.
The curfew is the same rule **Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson were suspended for breaching** earlier this year.
The three-match series against Pakistan begins **August 19**.
stories.background: England's Test set-up has been through turbulence this year: Ben Stokes retired in June during the New Zealand series, having earlier been suspended for a Test — along with pace bowler Gus Atkinson — for breaching the team's midnight curfew during a night out. Former coach Brendon McCullum also stepped down after England lost that series 2-1. Root, England's most-capped modern batter, has now returned to the Test captaincy he previously held, alongside a new coaching setup.
stories.what_happened: Root confirmed England will not operate under a curfew for the upcoming three-match Test series against Pakistan, arguing that if players are trusted to make good decisions on the field, they should be trusted to do the same off it. It's the first real decision of his reinstated captaincy, and directly reverses the disciplinary approach that led to Stokes and Atkinson's suspension earlier in the year. The series begins August 19.
stories.why_it_matters: It signals a deliberate cultural reset for an England dressing room that lost both its captain and its coach in the space of a few months — trading top-down discipline for personal responsibility right as a new leadership era begins.
stories.ripple_effects: The decision will be watched closely if England's on-field form or off-field discipline slips during the series — it sets an early tone for how the Root-Fleming era manages the team.
stories.why_now: It comes a week before the series opener, as Root settles into the captaincy and puts his own stamp on the team.
stories.watch_next: How England perform — and behave off the field — once the series against Pakistan starts on August 19.
stories.the_lesson: New leaders often reveal their approach first through small symbolic decisions — how a captain handles team culture says as much about their style as their tactics do.

stories.title: Hasan Mahmud's career-best 6-for stuns Australia as Bangladesh's pacers bowl them out for 198 in Darwin
key_points: Bangladesh bowled Australia out for just **198** on day one of the first Test in Darwin.
**Hasan Mahmud** took a career-best **6 for 55** — his third Test five-wicket haul.
Bangladesh's **fast bowlers took all 10 Australian wickets** — only the second time that's happened in the team's Test history.
**Steven Smith** top-scored for Australia with **71 off 109 balls**.
It's Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.
stories.background: Bangladesh has not played a Test series in Australia in 23 years, making this tour a rare and significant assignment for a team more often associated with home conditions and spin bowling than fast bowling on the road. The first Test began August 13 at Marrara Stadium in Darwin and runs through August 17.
stories.what_happened: Australia won the toss and chose to bat first at Marrara Stadium in Darwin, but were bowled out for 198 by the end of the first day. Hasan Mahmud led the destruction with a career-best 6 for 55 — his third Test five-wicket haul — while Taskin Ahmed and Ebadot Hossain chipped in with two wickets each. It marked only the second time in Bangladesh's Test history that fast bowlers have taken all 10 wickets in an innings, after a similar feat in Rawalpindi in 2024. Steven Smith was the one bright spot for Australia, top-scoring with 71 off 109 balls including seven fours and a six.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a statement performance from a Bangladesh fast-bowling attack that has historically been considered the weaker part of its bowling arsenal compared to its spinners — and it came on just the first day of the team's first Test tour of Australia in over two decades.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong start with the ball puts pressure on Bangladesh's own batting lineup to make the most of it when they take strike, and could reshape how seriously opponents take Bangladesh's pace bowling on future away tours.
stories.why_now: It's day one of a five-day Test running through August 17, so this is just the opening chapter of the series — but a dominant one.
stories.watch_next: How Bangladesh's batters respond when they take strike, and whether the pace attack can back up this display for the rest of the match.

key_terms.definition: A bowler taking five or more wickets in a single innings — considered a standout individual bowling performance in cricket.

stories.the_lesson: Home advantage isn't automatic — a well-drilled bowling attack exploiting helpful conditions can undo even a strong batting lineup on its own turf.

stories.title: A record 231-run stand powers Afghanistan to a series-sealing 42-run win over Ireland

thread.previously: We reported Afghanistan had already secured a direct spot at the 2027 Cricket World Cup by beating Ireland in their ongoing ODI series.
thread.changed: Afghanistan has now won the 4th ODI too, by 42 runs, built on a record 231-run partnership between Ibrahim Zadran and Sediqullah Atal — extending their lead to an unassailable 3-0 with one match left.

key_points: Afghanistan beat Ireland by **42 runs** in the 4th ODI in Belfast, posting **343 for 9**.
**Ibrahim Zadran and Sediqullah Atal put on 231 runs** together — Afghanistan's highest-ever 2nd-wicket stand in ODIs.
**Sediqullah Atal scored 143** off 120 balls and was named Player of the Match.
Ireland fought back with **Andy Balbirnie (109)** and Curtis Campher (84), but fell short chasing 344.
The win gives Afghanistan an **unassailable 3-0 lead** in the five-match series, with one game left to play.
stories.background: Afghanistan's cricket team has become one of the format's most dangerous white-ball sides in recent years, built around explosive batting and world-class spin from players like Rashid Khan. This series in Ireland matters beyond bragging rights: Afghanistan had already used an earlier win in the series to lock in a direct qualification spot for the 2027 ODI Cricket World Cup, so these later matches are as much about form and momentum as they are about the series scoreline itself.
stories.what_happened: Afghanistan posted a commanding **343 for 9** in the 4th ODI at Belfast's Civil Service Cricket Club, anchored by a **231-run partnership** between **Ibrahim Zadran** and **Sediqullah Atal** — the highest second-wicket stand in Afghanistan's ODI history. Atal top-scored with **143 off 120 balls** and was named Player of the Match, while Ireland's McDonough (3 for 84) and Hoey (2 for 71) did what damage they could. Chasing 344, Ireland put up a real fight through half-centuries from **Andy Balbirnie (109)** and Curtis Campher (84), but fell 42 runs short, finishing on 301. Afghanistan's bowlers, led by **Yamin Ahmadzai (4 for 71)** and spin great **Rashid Khan (3 for 49)**, closed out the win. The result gives Afghanistan an **unassailable 3-0 lead** in the five-match series, with the fifth and final ODI still to come.
stories.why_it_matters: This isn't just a routine series win — Afghanistan piling up its highest-ever partnership for that wicket shows genuine batting depth developing behind its well-known bowling attack, which matters heading into a World Cup cycle where they've already qualified.
stories.ripple_effects: A dominant series like this builds momentum and confidence for Afghanistan ahead of the 2027 World Cup, and gives players like Atal a strong case for a settled middle-order spot. For Ireland, it's a tough series to take heading into their own World Cup qualification push, despite individual bright spots from Balbirnie and Campher.
stories.why_now: The 4th ODI was played on August 12, continuing a series that started earlier this month, with just the fifth and final match remaining.
stories.watch_next: The fifth and final ODI, where Ireland will look for a consolation win and Afghanistan will aim to complete a series whitewash.
stories.the_lesson: A single record partnership can change the entire shape of a match — big totals in limited-overs cricket usually trace back to one long stand where batters kept the scoreboard moving without losing wickets, rather than even scoring throughout the innings.

stories.title: Australia win the toss and bat first as the historic Bangladesh Test begins in Darwin

thread.previously: We reported Australia was set to reunite its Cummins-Starc-Hazlewood pace attack for the first Bangladesh Test, with the hosts still finalizing their XI amid fitness 'niggles' in camp.
thread.changed: Play has now actually started: captain Pat Cummins won the toss and chose to bat first on a green, humid Darwin pitch, and Australia's confirmed XI includes both Cameron Green and Beau Webster, plus a returning Nathan Lyon, while Bangladesh has picked Ebadot Hossain and Mahmudul Hasan.

key_points: Australia captain **Pat Cummins won the toss** and chose to **bat first** on a green, humid Darwin pitch.
The confirmed Australia XI includes **Cameron Green and Beau Webster**, both winning selection battles for the spot.
**Nathan Lyon returns** after missing the back end of the Ashes with a hamstring injury.
The Cummins-Hazlewood-Starc pace trio is playing together for the **first time in more than a year**.
This is Bangladesh's **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**, marking a historic return fixture.
stories.background: Bangladesh last toured Australia for a Test series back in 2003, when Australia won comfortably — so this five-day match at Darwin's Marrara Cricket Ground, starting the current series, is being treated as a genuinely historic fixture for Bangladeshi cricket. Australia has been juggling injuries and form questions in its bowling attack over the past year, including during the recent Ashes series, which is why the reunion of its three most experienced fast bowlers together is being watched closely.
stories.what_happened: Australia won the toss and captain **Pat Cummins** elected to bat first on a green Darwin surface in humid conditions, with opener **Travis Head** expecting a tough opening period against the new ball. Australia's confirmed XI is: Jake Weatherald, Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins (captain), Nathan Lyon, and Josh Hazlewood. stories.why_it_matters: This is a milestone fixture for Bangladesh cricket regardless of the result, and for Australia it's the first real test of whether their full-strength pace attack can stay fit and effective together after a stretch of individual injuries and rotation.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong showing from Bangladesh would be a meaningful confidence boost for a team still building credibility in Test cricket outside home conditions, while Australia's results here feed directly into broader questions about squad depth heading into the next World Test Championship cycle.
